nameStory: The species name 'ammophilus' comes from Greek words meaning 'sand-loving,' hinting at this jumping spider's preference for sandy habitats. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name yet, you might think of it as the Sand-loving Jumping Spider based on its scientific moniker.
description: This is a small jumping spider in the Attulus genus, part of the charismatic jumping spider family known for their excellent vision and hunting prowess. Like other jumping spiders, it has a compact, robust body with relatively short legs compared to web-building spiders. Adults typically measure about 3-5mm in body length, making them quite small even by jumping spider standards. They have the characteristic large forward-facing eyes that give jumping spiders their alert, almost curious appearance.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large eyes arranged in a front row, with the middle pair being particularly prominent and giving an almost telescope-like appearance - these gleam like tiny black jewels when light hits them

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and sturdy build typical of jumping spiders, with a relatively flat carapace (front section) that feels firm if gently touched, and short, stocky legs

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small at 3-5mm body length - about the size of a pencil eraser or small ladybug, easily overlooked unless you're looking carefully

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with sudden stops, often turning to look directly at you when approached - no web building, hunts actively by stalking prey

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates only small silk retreats or safety lines, not webs for catching prey - you might find tiny silk shelters under rocks or in crevices

habitat: **Note: Habitat details are uncertain due to limited data** - Likely found in sandy or well-drained soils based on its scientific name, possibly in coastal areas, sandy riverbanks, or open areas with loose substrate. Given the single observation record, this species may be quite rare in New England or easily overlooked due to its small size.

seasonality.spring: **Uncertain** - Adults may begin appearing as temperatures warm, potentially emerging from overwintering retreats in sandy soils or under rocks.
seasonality.summer: **Uncertain** - Likely most active period for hunting and reproduction, when you'd be most likely to spot individuals basking on warm sandy surfaces.
seasonality.fall: **Uncertain** - May still be active in early fall, possibly preparing overwintering sites or laying egg sacs in protected sandy locations.
seasonality.winter: **Uncertain** - Probably inactive, sheltering in silk-lined retreats under rocks, logs, or in sandy substrate to survive freezing temperatures.

funFact: **Uncertain claim** - Like other jumping spiders, this tiny arachnid can see in color and may actually have better color vision than humans, with the ability to see into the UV spectrum - imagine experiencing the world through eyes that can detect rainbow patterns on flowers that are completely invisible to us!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded observation in New England, this species is most likely to be confused with other small jumping spiders in the region. The key is focusing on the sandy habitat preference and very small size - most other jumping spiders you'll encounter will be noticeably larger or found in different habitats like gardens or wooded areas.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents how much we still don't know about New England's smaller arachnids - with only one recorded observation, it highlights the importance of careful observation and documentation by citizen scientists. Many tiny jumping spiders are likely more common than records suggest, simply because they're easily overlooked.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives like the Asiatic Wall Jumping Spider, this species appears to prefer sandy habitats rather than human structures. The Downy Jumping Spider and Flower Jumping Spider are typically found in more vegetated areas, while ammophilus seems adapted to more open, sandy environments. **Note: These comparisons are based on limited data and scientific names, as detailed information about this species' characteristics in New England is scarce.**

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relatives in the Attulus genus, the Asiatic Wall Jumping Spider is more associated with artificial structures rather than natural habitats.

Among its Attulus relatives in New England, the downy jumping spider is distinguished by its particularly dense hair coating compared to the Asiatic wall jumping spider, which has a smoother appearance.
The Flower Jumping Spider is smaller and more flower-focused than its relatives like the Asiatic Wall Jumping Spider, which prefers vertical surfaces like walls and tree trunks.
